mainEntity.name: How to calculate markup on food?

acceptedAnswer.text: Put the cost on the pounds you can sell, then mark that up. A $48.00 case at 40 lb and an 85% yield gives 34 usable lb, so cost is $1.41 a lb, and a 32% target margin prices it at $2.08. Mark up the $1.20 you paid per bought pound instead and you get $1.76, which leaves the trim unpaid for.

mainEntity.name: How much mark up should you charge on food?

acceptedAnswer.text: Enough to cover the trim, not a round number off a chart. On this case $22.72 of gross profit against a $48.00 cost is a 47.3% markup, and the same $22.72 against $70.72 of revenue is a 32.1% margin. Decide the margin the line has to carry, then read off the markup it needs.

mainEntity.name: Does trim belong in the cost or in the markup?

acceptedAnswer.text: In the cost, not the markup. Spread the $48.00 case over the 34 lb you can sell and cost is $1.41 a usable lb. Mark that up to $2.08. Price off the 40 lb you bought and the same target gives $1.76, which is $0.32 a lb short.

mainEntity.name: How do you calculate food cost on product you cut yourself?

acceptedAnswer.text: Divide the case cost by the usable pounds, not the pounds on the invoice. $48.00 over 34 usable lb is $1.41, against $1.20 over the 40 lb you bought. The food cost percentage then comes off what the case really earns, so $48.00 of $70.72 is 67.9%.

mainEntity.name: Is trim the same as shrink?

acceptedAnswer.text: No, and they belong in different places. Shrink is product you lose to spoilage, damage or a short count, and it goes into your landed cost. Trim is weight you never intended to sell, 6 lb of every 40 lb case here, and it belongs in the price per pound. Budgeting for one does not cover the other.

mainEntity.name: How does yield change the price you need?

acceptedAnswer.text: Every point of yield you lose is carried by the pounds that are left. At an 85% yield this case needs $2.08 a lb. At 75% it needs $2.35, and at 90% it needs $1.96, a $0.39 spread on the same $48.00 case. Yield moves the price more than the case cost usually does.

mainEntity.name: What yield should you use on a cut item?

acceptedAnswer.text: Your own, measured. Weigh the case in, weigh the saleable product out, and do it across a few cases and a few cutters. Assume 85% and really get 75% and you sell 30 lb at a price built for 34, so the case earns $62.40 instead of $70.72 and the margin goes with it.
